title: Sleep Pathways Guild — PLMS versus PAP pressure escalation (RPSGT Domain 2)

sourceReview.book: Mattice, Brooks, & Lee-Chiong (Eds.), Fundamentals of Sleep Technology (3rd ed., 2020), Chapter 48 and Chapter 41
sourceReview.note: Primary PAP titration goals are obstructive apneas, hypopneas, RERAs and snoring. Exploratory adjustment may address flow limitation; PLMS alone do not authorize pressure increase.

duplicateScreening: Compared conceptually with D2B/D2C/D3A task modules and October 11 owner-release PLMS prompts. Complete 3,240-record semantic family review and learner-history regression remain pending.

questions.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
questions.prompt: An adult's obstructive apneas, hypopneas, RERAs and snoring are controlled during CPAP titration, with no remaining inspiratory flow flattening. Periodic leg movements and some associated EEG arousals continue. What should the technologist do next?
options: Increase CPAP whenever a series of leg movements appears
Keep pressure stable, document the limb movements and arousals, and follow the laboratory's titration protocol
Switch immediately to bilevel PAP to suppress the leg movements
Add supplemental oxygen because periodic leg movements persist
questions.answer: Keep pressure stable, document the limb movements and arousals, and follow the laboratory's titration protocol
questions.rationale: Manual PAP titration targets obstructive apneas, hypopneas, RERAs and snoring. Isolated PLMS, even when accompanied by arousals, are not independent pressure-escalation criteria. Record the movements, arousals, respiratory control and pressure; follow the physician-approved laboratory protocol. Excess pressure can itself cause arousals or central respiratory events.

distractorRationales.Increase CPAP whenever a series of leg m: A leg-movement series is not a listed PAP escalation criterion.
distractorRationales.Switch immediately to bilevel PAP to sup: Bilevel PAP changes are based on respiratory treatment and tolerance indications, not PLMS alone.
distractorRationales.Add supplemental oxygen because periodic: Oxygen is not a treatment for isolated PLMS and is not indicated solely by their presence.

questions.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
questions.prompt: During PAP titration, a leg movement occurs at the end of several flow-limited breaths with increasing respiratory effort and an EEG arousal. The breath sequence does not meet apnea or hypopnea criteria. Which finding could support a protocol-based increase in PAP?
options: A qualifying respiratory effort-related arousal (RERA), after reviewing the respiratory signals and applicable titration thresholds
The number of leg movements regardless of respiratory signals
The patient's periodic limb movement index alone
questions.answer: A qualifying respiratory effort-related arousal (RERA), after reviewing the respiratory signals and applicable titration thresholds
questions.rationale: A RERA is a respiratory disturbance associated with arousal and is a recognized PAP titration target. Evaluate the flow contour, respiratory effort and arousal before attributing the event to an independent limb movement. Pressure is increased when qualifying obstructive respiratory findings meet the physician-approved protocol, not because leg EMG activity is present.

distractorRationales.The tibialis EMG burst itself: A limb movement is not by itself a respiratory titration trigger.
distractorRationales.The number of leg movements regardless o: Periodic leg movements cannot replace respiratory-event assessment.
distractorRationales.The patient's periodic limb movement ind: The PLM index documents movement frequency, not the PAP pressure needed to open the airway.

questions.task: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
questions.prompt: Obstructive apneas, hypopneas, RERAs and snoring have been eliminated during CPAP titration. The PAP flow waveform still shows inspiratory flattening, and intermittent PLMS are also present. If limited exploratory pressure increases are permitted by the laboratory protocol, what is the appropriate rationale to document?
options: The patient has any leg movements during sleep
Persistent inspiratory flow flattening indicating possible residual upper-airway resistance, rather than the PLMS
Each PLM-associated arousal requires an automatic CPAP increase
PAP pressure should always rise until no arousals of any cause remain
questions.answer: Persistent inspiratory flow flattening indicating possible residual upper-airway resistance, rather than the PLMS
questions.rationale: The AASM titration guidance allows limited exploration above the pressure controlling obstructive events for residual flow limitation and sleep continuity. That is an airway-related assessment, not treatment of PLMS. Document the respiratory finding, response and physician-approved protocol limits; do not frame isolated limb movements as a pressure criterion.

distractorRationales.The patient has any leg movements during: Presence of PLMS does not determine PAP pressure.
distractorRationales.Each PLM-associated arousal requires an: Arousals due to nonrespiratory causes do not establish residual obstruction.
distractorRationales.PAP pressure should always rise until no: Unnecessary pressure can worsen comfort or create sleep disruption; titration follows defined respiratory goals.

questions.prompt: A patient has frequent periodic leg movements with arousals while breathing remains adequately controlled on stable CPAP. Which technologist note best supports interpretation of the titration?
options: 'CPAP increased for every limb movement; no respiratory details needed'
'At stable CPAP, obstructive respiratory events remained controlled; periodic leg movements and associated arousals continued and were documented for physician review'
'The patient has confirmed periodic limb movement disorder; no further assessment needed'
'Leg EMG activity was ignored because CPAP was working'
questions.answer: 'At stable CPAP, obstructive respiratory events remained controlled; periodic leg movements and associated arousals continued and were documented for physician review'
questions.rationale: The technologist should record the effective pressure, respiratory findings and persistent limb movements/arousals without diagnosing PLMD or adjusting PAP solely for PLMS. Accurate notes help the interpreting clinician distinguish residual respiratory sleep fragmentation from a coexisting movement finding.

distractorRationales.'CPAP increased for every limb movement;: Pressure changes require justified respiratory or protocol indications and clear documentation.
distractorRationales.'The patient has confirmed periodic limb: A PLMS finding on PSG alone does not establish PLMD, and diagnosis is outside this technologist action.
distractorRationales.'Leg EMG activity was ignored because CP: Persistent movements and associated arousals are clinically relevant observations to document.
